items.t: Canadian Natural Resources vs. Enbridge: The Better Dividend Stock to Buy Today
sum: When it comes to dividend investing, Canadian Natural Resources (TSX: CNQ) and Enbridge (TSX: ENB) are two top names worth watching. Both these energy companies have impressive payout records, consistently paying and increasing their dividends over the years. Their strong asset bases, well-established businesses, and ability to generate healthy cash flow have helped them reward shareholders through different market conditions.

However, despite their similarities as reliable dividend payers, the two companies operate quite differently. This also means they offer investors different opportunities and come with different risks.

Canadian Natural Resources is one of Canada’s major oil and natural gas producers. Its operations span across Western Canada, the U.K. North Sea, and offshore Africa. One of its biggest strengths is its large reserve base and long-life, low-decline assets, which support steady production over time. Moreover, CNQ can benefit significantly when oil and natural gas prices are strong, although its earnings and cash flow are also more exposed to commodity price fluctuations.

Enbridge, on the other hand, operates a very different business. It operates an extensive network of liquid pipelines, natural gas utilities, and other energy infrastructure assets. Much of its revenue comes from regulated operations and long-term contracts, allowing it to generate relatively stable and predictable cash flow. This makes Enbridge particularly attractive to investors looking for dependable dividend income and less exposure to swings in commodity prices.

So, while both companies have a history of rewarding shareholders, their investment appeal differs. Canadian Natural Resources offers greater exposure to energy prices and potential upside when commodity markets are favourable, whereas Enbridge provides a more infrastructure-focused business with relatively predictable cash flows.
Before comparing their growth prospects and deciding which stock could be the better buy today, let’s first take a closer look at their dividend payment histories.

Canadian Natural Resources and Enbridge stand out as top dividend payers and growers. CNQ recently increased its quarterly dividend to $0.63 per share, representing its 26th consecutive annual increase in 2026.

sum: Canadian Natural Resources shifted investor attention from its third-quarter earnings to the durability of its capital-return plan after management said on Thursday, November 5, that buybacks could continue at a similar pace into 2027 if free cash flow remains strong. The comment adds a forward-looking detail to the company's plan to direct 100% of free cash flow to repurchases, subject to market conditions.

On the earnings call, President Scott Stauth said the planned monthly repurchase pace should not be viewed as a two-month trial. He expects the company to continue at a similar rate into the new year while commodity prices and free cash flow remain supportive. The full transcript is available from Yahoo Finance.

Canadian Natural reached its CAD 13 billion net debt target earlier than expected, ending the quarter at CAD 12.1 billion. The company targets CAD 800 million of share repurchases in each of November and December, while management said the pace could change if commodity prices shift materially.

The Horizon oil sands turnaround was completed in 28 days, seven days ahead of schedule. Management expects the earlier completion to add 23,000 barrels per day of high-margin synthetic crude production in the fourth quarter and has extended the planned interval between turnarounds from two years to three years.

Canadian Natural also reported record quarterly thermal in situ production of approximately 300,000 barrels per day and record North American conventional liquids production of approximately 358,000 barrels per day. Management expects a strong fourth quarter, supported by oil sands mining and upgrading, thermal operations and execution across its portfolio.

sum: Canadian Natural Resources is approaching its third-quarter report with expectations for stronger year-over-year earnings, but the preview from Zacks Equity Research, published by Yahoo Finance on November 3, does not point to a clear earnings beat. The company is scheduled to release results before the market opens on Thursday, November 5.

Zacks puts its third-quarter estimate at 1.05 dollars per share and revenue of 8.3 billion dollars. The earnings estimate is 69.4 percent above the year-earlier level, while the revenue forecast implies 20 percent growth. At the same time, the earnings consensus has been reduced by 7.9 percent over the past 30 days, raising the importance of the final operating figures.

Canadian Natural Resources enters the release after adjusted earnings per share of 1.58 dollars in the second quarter, above the 1.43-dollar consensus estimate cited by Zacks. Second-quarter revenue was reported at 10.6 billion dollars against a 9.2-billion-dollar estimate. Zacks said the company had exceeded consensus earnings estimates in each of the previous four quarters, with an average surprise of 12.9 percent.

The preview identifies several potential supports for the quarter. Canadian Natural Resources has raised its 2026 production guidance, while output from Jackfish and volumes from acquired assets could bolster earnings. Operating efficiencies and possible cost savings of 10 percent or more at Peace River may also support profitability.

Commodity pricing remains a counterweight. Management expects synthetic crude pricing to moderate from the second quarter premium of 8.37 dollars per barrel over West Texas Intermediate toward parity or a modest premium. That shift could reduce realized prices and profitability. Planned maintenance extending through the third quarter and into early fourth quarter may also constrain production and lift expenses.

Zacks also points to the company's capital expenditure program of approximately 6 billion Canadian dollars for 2026. Weaker commodity prices would increase pressure on free cash flow, although the preview says operating improvements could provide support. Its model does not conclusively predict an earnings beat for this release.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index, the main benchmark of the Toronto Stock Exchange, closed at 35,801.09 on Monday, up 181.06 points or 0.51% from Friday's close of 35,620.03. The blue-chip S&P/TSX 60 rose 0.49% to 2,135.53.

The index gave back roughly half of its earlier gains. It was up more than 330 points at around 35,950 in early afternoon, before easing as US technology stocks turned lower. Even so, Toronto outperformed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, both of which finished in negative territory, helped by its smaller exposure to large technology companies.

Financials, materials, industrials and real estate led the advance, with Royal Bank of Canada up 0.8% and Bank of Montreal up 1.1%. Gold recovered from recent lows, with December futures up 1.35% to $3,951.50 an ounce, supporting miners after last week's heavy selling. Trade news provided an additional boost: President Donald Trump said his administration had set up a framework for a new trade agreement with Canada, and Prime Minister Mark Carney described the discussions as constructive. Formal negotiations are expected to resume this week.

Domestic data also helped. Ottawa's federal deficit narrowed to C$223 million in August as revenues rose 7.1%, easing concerns about government borrowing. The top gainers were spread across sectors. Colliers International rose 7.90% to C$145.98, Aecon Group climbed 7.84% to C$53.09 and Curaleaf Holdings gained 8.50% to C$12.77. Industrial and construction names benefited from improving trade sentiment and lower fuel costs.

TC Energy also has a solid investment pipeline. Its $22 billion secured capital program through 2031 will support its earnings growth and dividend payouts.

TC Energy’s relatively predictable cash flow, a long record of dividend increases, exposure to growing natural gas demand, and a substantial pipeline of secured projects make it a reliable income stock.

sum: There's a saying on Wall Street: "Dividends don't lie." Just about every financial metric can be fudged or spun by management, but the dividends either arrive in a brokerage account, or they don't. Since 2000, the S&P 500 companies have grown their payouts by 376%, or an average of 4.76% each year.

That's kept ahead of the 92% inflation seen in that time frame. Still, after over 25 years, it's nothing to write home about. Thankfully, some companies have offered income growth that's orders of magnitude greater. Coming in near the top of the list is Calgary-based oil and gas firm Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ -1.05%).

In 2001, Canadian Natural Resources began paying a dividend of $0.00625 per share, with the payout tripling within five years. By 2011, its dividend had grown by 620% since 2001's payouts, and by 2021, its dividend had mushroomed 553% from 2011's levels. Today, its quarterly payouts are up exactly 100% from those of five years ago.

Since 2001, not only has the company raised its dividend every year, but it's done so by an average of 21% each year. All told, its dividend has grown 9,300% since 2001. Of the hundreds of income stocks I've analyzed over the years, I've never seen a company like this.

Canadian Natural Resources generated an operating cash flow of $14.8 billion last year, which easily covers the $3.6 billion needed to pay its current dividend. In fact, the company could grow its payouts by another 21% in 2026, and still have over $10 billion in operating cash flow left over.

An expected energy glut could put pressure on earnings, but the company can be profitable as long as oil prices are above $21 per barrel (thanks to its industry-leading operating costs). And even if growth slows, the company's current dividend yield of 4.3% is almost quadruple the S&P 500 average. For investors seeking fast-growing, dependable income, Canadian Natural Resources is a top candidate.

sum: Shares of Canada's largest oil producers fell on Monday, as markets opened for the first time since the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by U.S. forces over the weekend.
America is now set to gain control of the Latin American nation's battered heavy oil industry. For Canada, the move could put pressure on its oil exports to its southern neighbour.

Canadian producers Suncor Energy (SU.TO)(SU), Imperial Oil (IMO.TO)(IMO), Cenovus Energy (CVE.TO)(CVE), and Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ.TO)(CNQ) saw their stocks fall on Monday. Meanwhile, shares of their American counterparts, like ExxonMobil (XOM) and Chevron Corporation (CVX), moved in the opposite direction.
Canada's iShares S&P/TSX Capped Energy Index ETF (XEG.TO) fell as much as 6.3 per cent on Monday, before closing down 3.43 per cent.

"America's capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro on January 3 — with control over the country's oil sector a core objective of the military operation — constitutes a longer-term structural risk for oil prices in general, and Canada's heavy oil export markets in particular," RBC Capital Markets analyst Greg Pardy wrote in a note to clients on Sunday night.

"But restoring the country's production back towards the three million [barrel per day] range would require years of annual investment of some $10 billion, anchored by a stable security environment — both of which are tall orders."

Canada's main heavy oil benchmark, Western Canadian Select (WCS), is priced at a discount to America's light oil benchmark, known as West Texas Intermediate. The difference reflects Canada's heavier grade, as well as transportation costs, and other factors. The start of the Trans Mountain Pipeline Expansion Project last summer has shrunk this discount to its tightest range in over a decade.

Returns Are Gaining Momentum At Canadian Natural Resources (TSE:CNQ)
sum: Did you know there are some financial metrics that can provide clues of a potential multi-bagger? Firstly, we'd want to identify a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and then alongside that, an ever-increasing base of capital employed. If you see this, it typically means it's a company with a great business model and plenty of profitable reinvestment opportunities. Speaking of which, we noticed some great changes in Canadian Natural Resources' (TSE:CNQ) returns on capital, so let's have a look.

For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for Canadian Natural Resources, this is the formula:
Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)
0.11 = CA$8.9b ÷ (CA$86b - CA$8.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to September 2025).
Thus, Canadian Natural Resources has an ROCE of 11%. On its own, that's a standard return, however it's much better than the 8.4% generated by the Oil and Gas industry.
What Can We Tell From Canadian Natural Resources' ROCE Trend?

Canadian Natural Resources' ROCE growth is quite impressive. More specifically, while the company has kept capital employed relatively flat over the last five years, the ROCE has climbed 2,242% in that same time. Basically the business is generating higher returns from the same amount of capital and that is proof that there are improvements in the company's efficiencies. It's worth looking deeper into this though because while it's great that the business is more efficient, it might also mean that going forward the areas to invest internally for the organic growth are lacking.

items.t: The Absolute Best Canadian Stocks to Buy and Hold Forever in a TFSA
sum: The best stocks to buy anytime are the dividend kings, who never have to worry about demand. Other stocks are worth buying at a better value than at their all-time highs. And if you are looking for a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) investment that you can buy for a longer term, you need to look at companies that can thrive in a crisis and grow in a healthy economy.

The best stocks to invest in are those that are major contributors to the Canadian economy. The strength of the export-led Canadian economy is in mining and oil reserves and the technology, finance, and logistics infrastructure it has built to export these reserves. Remember, exports will only be beneficial when the cost of exporting them is low.

The Russia-Ukraine war has created a natural gas export opportunity for Canada and increased natural gas prices. This shifting trend has created a buy-and-hold opportunity throughout the supply chain.

One of the biggest beneficiaries of this long-term shift in the supply chain was Tourmaline Oil (TSX:TOU), Canada's largest natural gas producer. The company has been producing natural gas since 2008, but it achieved the scale to distribute dividends in 2018. Natural gas presents a mid-ground for the transition from oil to renewables. The opening of the European market to Canadian natural gas in 2022 led to special dividends. While the natural gas prices have normalized, the export opportunity is here to stay.

Pipeline stocks like Enbridge and TC Energy (TSX:TRP) are also tapping the liquified natural gas (LNG) export opportunity by accelerating gas pipeline projects. TC Energy even spun off its oil pipeline business to focus on gas pipelines and has brought online US$8 billion of assets into service in the first nine months of 2025. It has sanctioned three more natural gas pipeline projects, which are expected to deliver 5.9 times the weighted average build cost with its 20-year service contract.

The on-budget and timely completion of pipelines has improved TC Energy's operating efficiency. Moreover, it will be the beneficiary of the Canadian government's support in LNG Canada Phase II as the nation looks to expand export partners. You can buy and forget TC Energy stock even when it trades near its high.

items.t: The Canadian Stock That Hedge Fund Managers Can’t Get Enough of
A Dividend Giant I’d Buy Over Enbridge Stock Right Now
sum: Whenever there is a mention of dividends, the first name that pops up in every Canadian's mind is Enbridge (TSX:ENB). The pipeline company earned this status from its 60-plus years of dividend-paying history and a 30-year dividend growth history.

Enbridge has increased its debt to 4.8 times Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization (EBITDA). The higher leverage ratio is because of major acquisitions, which increased revenue but also costs. The purchases have slowed its dividend growth rate to 3% as it focuses on reducing leverage and transitioning to gas pipelines. It expects to accelerate the dividend growth rate to 5% after 2026.

The acquisitions have increased Enbridge's share price range from $40–$60 to $60–$70, reducing its dividend yield to 5.5%. Those who invested in it at around a $45–$50 share price will continue to enjoy a higher yield of over 7.5%. It is a stock to hold for its dividend yield. However, it may not be the most attractive dividend stock to buy at the current price point of $68.25, just 3% below its 52-week high.

Canada is looking to tap new export markets amidst tense trade relations with the United States. The market has already priced in the natural gas export opportunity, leaving little upside for Enbridge's share price. However, there is a risk of downside if tariffs are prolonged.
The 5.5% yield, slow dividend growth, high leverage, and limited share price upside make Enbridge less attractive right now.

A better energy stock alternative to Enbridge in the current market is Canadian Natural Resources (TSX:CNQ). Analysts remain bullish on Canadian Natural Resources, citing its strong capital allocation strategy as a key driver of potential upside. The company has operational discipline, strong execution, and capital allocation transparency.
CNQ incorporates the dividend amount into its breakeven price, which is mid-$40/barrel on WTI. This cost advantage, combined with regular share buybacks, helps it grow dividends between 2% and 56%.
